text.en: Imagine sitting under a tree and hearing it whisper to you. In this play-like conversation, a girl called Amber talks to the old neem tree in her courtyard, and the tree turns out to be a wise teacher. Let us find out what Neem Baba has to say.

Trees are useful in many ways. We use their parts for medicines, wood, fruit, shade and more. The book asks what you already know about the neem tree and what you want to know. Use that to read actively.
Amber returns from school and sits in the shade of the neem tree in her courtyard. It seems to whisper to her, so she greets it politely with namaste. Neem Baba says he knows her, because she played in his shade as a child, and she may call him Neem Baba. He says he is very old. He was born millions of years ago in North India or Myanmar, and his family soon spread outside India to many countries of Asia, Africa and even parts of America.
In India neem was given Sanskrit names such as Arishta, which means one who cures diseases, along with Nimba and Nimbaca. The name Neem was given by the Iranians. In Hindi it is Nimb. Other names are Nim, Leemba, Nimori, Nimbamond, Nimbe and Nimo. Neem Baba says we become well known by what we do. Scientists call neem bitter grace of God, nature's gift to man and cleanliness-parting tree. Some call it magic tree and tree of the twentieth century.
Neem twigs are used to clean teeth, and the leaves protect clothes. When someone has measles, doctors suggest putting neem leaves on the bed. Neem leaves have chemical properties that destroy germs. They give comfort from itching and do not allow germs to grow. Leaves, bark, flowers, fruit and even roots can be used to make medicines. Amber says her grandmother cured her cough with medicine from neem bark and cured her father's itching eyes with kajal from neem flowers. Neem Baba gives an important warning: these remedies are only for people who are well trained and have a lot of experience, so do not try them on your own.
If neem seed powder is mixed with water and sprayed on plants and trees, locusts do not eat them. Locusts are flying insects that damage crops. In rice fields where water stands, neem stops mosquito breeding and helps the crop yield. It also saves crops from termites, which eat roots, and stops other insects from breeding. Amber realises that putting neem seed powder in the stagnant water around homes would stop mosquitoes, and it is a cost-effective method.
Stored grains are kept safe from insects by adding neem seed powder. Neem oil is used to make soap and toothpaste. Furniture made of neem wood is not eaten by termites, and neem also purifies the air. Neem Baba says there are many qualities still to be discovered, and asks Amber to discover them when she grows up. She promises she will. The story is called thought-provoking because even a common tree has an interesting history and countless uses, so it makes us think about how valuable nature is.
A compound word is made of two words joined together. Open compounds have a space, such as neem oil and seed powder. Closed compounds have no space, such as grandmother, childhood and something. Hyphenated compounds use a hyphen, such as well-known, well-trained and thought-provoking. Verbs change in the past. Become becomes became, find becomes found, make becomes made, discover becomes discovered, tell becomes told, give becomes gave. Example: I want to become a teacher when I grow up. Another: Amber found many facts from Neem Baba.
Personification gives human qualities to non-living things or nature. Amber speaks to the neem tree as if it were a person, and it answers. More examples: the leaves whispered in the wind; the flowers danced merrily in the breeze. Write a paragraph about a tree you like. Say where it is, how it looks and why you like it, and give your paragraph a title. Persians who saw this tree in India called it Azad Darakhte Hindi, and the scientific name of neem is Azadirachta indica.

problem.en: Match present verbs with the past: become, find, make, discover, tell, give.

text.en: Look at which are irregular, changing their spelling.

why.en: Become, find, make, tell and give change form.

text.en: Become - became, find - found, make - made, discover - discovered, tell - told, give - gave.

why.en: Discover is regular and adds ed.

problem.en: Sort into open, closed and hyphenated compounds: seed powder, grandmother, well-known.

text.en: Check how the two words are joined.
Seed powder is open, grandmother is closed and well-known is hyphenated.

why.en: The three types depend on how the words are separated.

prompt.en: Explain how neem is useful to people and farmers, and why Amber should not use remedies on her own.

requiredIdeas.en: Neem is used in medicines, toothpaste, soap and for cleaning teeth.
Farmers use seed powder to keep locusts, mosquitoes and termites away.
Neem leaves have chemical properties that destroy germs.
Only well-trained people with experience should prepare remedies.

commonMisconceptions.en: Neem is only useful for shade.

points.en: Neem Baba is a conversation between Amber and the neem tree.
Neem comes from India or Myanmar and is found in Asia, Africa and parts of America.
Its leaves, bark, flowers, fruit and roots are used for medicine; seed powder protects crops.
Medicines should be used only by trained people.
Compound words can be open, closed or hyphenated.
Personification gives human qualities to things in nature.
